thesis: This episode argues that Jack Henry (JKHY) is a highly regarded, customer-obsessed business with a strong culture of doing the right thing that drives long-term success. The speaker believes the company has normalized costs, sees tailwinds from M&A activity, and possesses a structural competitive advantage due to its scale, service ethos, and ability to modernize systems compared to legacy competitors. While the company is not very loved, it is expected to perform well in a tougher environment due to its security, reputation, and customer-centric approach.

claims.claim: The speaker believes Jack Henry has normalized costs and will see tailwinds from M&A activity, with a reasonable assumption of margin progression.
claims.quote: So that through a big hump of technology spends, IT costs and employee costs have normalized, the back end of COVID. So that's good. And then who knows, but it's a reasonable assumption. And potentially with the new administration in Washington, you're probably going to see a pick up an MNA activity. So those three are tailwinds.

claims.claim: The speaker thinks Jack Henry is now underpromising and overdelivering on margin assumptions compared to previous bullishness.
claims.quote: I think now they're saying 30, maybe 30, 40 basis points a year, wanting, I think, to underpromise, overdeliver. So that's how we look at it slow and steady margin progression over time.

claims.claim: The speaker views the consolidation of financial institutions as a tailwind for Jack Henry.
claims.quote: So you're obviously going to keep seeing consolidation because it's crazy to have 5,000 roughly financial institutions. So that's going to keep happening at the smaller end, as it has for a long period of time. So that's going to be on balance, a tail wind for Jack.

claims.claim: The speaker believes Jack Henry has the potential to move up the size curve into larger banks.
claims.quote: So I think that's one of the interesting things that could happen over the next few years is they start moving up the size change. So that'll be interesting to see how that develops over time. So generally the larger banks, that's more of the sweet spot would be for

claims.claim: The speaker thinks Jack Henry has room to move up the size curve by keeping architecture fresh and modern.
claims.quote: But over time, I think if you can keep your architecture fresh and modern, have core systems that I think there's room there's room there for Jack Henry to move up the size curve.

claims.claim: The speaker identifies cyber security and culture as the two main risks for Jack Henry.
claims.quote: I think it would be two risks. The number one obvious one is cyber security. So a major cyber security incident would be huge, obviously, for their reputation. All of these businesses run on reputation. And so if I'm a CTO or I'm a consultant, at the end of the day, I don't want to put my reputation's risk.

claims.claim: The speaker believes Jack Henry has a customer-centric culture that will go where the best solution is.
claims.quote: And the reason I say that, I don't have any strong evidence. But if I think of the customer-centric culture, they will go where the best solution is. And I think if they were to have a partner that could compromise them potentially, and then this is a really interesting thing that they've done.

claims.claim: The speaker thinks Jack Henry has a very good working relationship with MasterCard.
claims.quote: And do you have any sense of why that would be the case over a visa? I don't, actually, but it just appears that they have a very good relationship with them. I mean, obviously, obviously, MasterCard have the clearinghouse system, which is poor fast payments in the States.

claims.claim: The speaker believes Jack Henry has relationships with around 8,000 clients and financial institutions.
claims.quote: So they actually sell the complementary solutions to around 8,000 clients and financial institutions in the stage. So the relationship is there.

claims.claim: The speaker thinks Jack Henry has potential to move up the scale but not into the megabanks for core systems.
claims.quote: I just think there's potential for them to move up the scale. But into the megabanks, in terms of core, I don't think that's really where they want to go at this stage.

claims.claim: The speaker believes Jack Henry is a highly regarded business with a strong culture of customer obsession and employee care that drives long-term success.
claims.quote: I think the key one is really their culture and that customer obsession they have, that pride that they have in really looking after their customers. And sometimes that means taking a short-term profit hit to build the brand and the customer trust and the everything else that will pay off in spades over the long term.

claims.claim: The speaker states that Jack Henry is not very loved but will do well in a tougher environment due to its security and reputation.
claims.quote: And they said, well, it's quite interesting in times of excitement. They're in a little bit of excitement, nice, strong bull market at the moment. You know, we're not the most exciting stock. But in times of volatility, suddenly people really are willing to pay for that security that the stock has.

claims.claim: The speaker highlights that Jack Henry's culture of doing the right thing and having fun is a good way to run a business that has been demonstrated over the long term.
claims.quote: And I think that is such a good way to run a business. And it's there. You can see it's demonstrated over the long term. And I actually see another Midwest company is Sherwin Williams, which a completely different business. but they had that same thing.

claims.claim: The speaker believes that Jack Henry's focus on customers and employees will benefit shareholders in the long run, unlike businesses that focus on the quarter or year.
claims.quote: No, too often I think we see businesses where they put the shareholders first or they're trying to make the quarter or trying to make the year. but actually in the long run, shareholders don't benefit from that, nor to customers, nor to employees. I think that's the thing that I take for them.

claims.claim: The company has a structural competitive advantage due to its scale, service ethos, and ability to modernize systems compared to legacy competitors.
claims.quote: So not just against the other players like FyServe and Fidelity, which have tried to modernize their systems over the last couple of years, but then you've got this long tail as well of other software providers. Do you have a sense of what the average contract pricing looks like?

claims.claim: The company's private cloud solution offers significant benefits to customers, including better cyber security, margin uplift, and allowing them to 'sleep better at night' regarding risk and compliance.
claims.quote: So private cloud, that is hosted on Jack Henry's premises. So you've just taken the information that's sitting on your premises. You've just taken all of that information and stuck it on Jack Henry's service. Public Cloud, we're going to give it to Google or Amazon or Azure. So that's a totally different situation. But from Jack Henry's point of view, there's going to be better cyber security.

claims.claim: The company has a strong market position with just under 50% market share in the credit union space and about 25% in the banking sector.
claims.quote: So obviously, you've got some really big banks in America. So let's just talk about anything less than 50 billion. So within the credit union space, they've got just under 50% market share. And that's through their credit union solution, core solution, which is called Simitar. And then within the banking sector, about 25% market share.

claims.claim: The company has a 'nice runway' for growth driven by GDP, economic progress, and natural growth in assets and transactions.
claims.quote: So you can just see this nice runway. It's just such a nice way of growing off the back of GDP and economic progress, if you like. We've mentioned it a few times now. I am just thinking about the shift of going from on-premise to cloud and what that might entail.
